newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia aside, old foes welcome Clinton NATO pledge.
newsitem.headline: Russia aside, old foes welcome Clinton NATO pledge.

text.p: With the notable but unsurprising exception of Russia, NATO's old communist foes on Wednesday welcomed U.S. President Bill Clinton's pledge to bring new members into the Atlantic alliance by 1999.
But what would have been revolutionary a few years ago failed to trigger jubilation -- a reflection of how firmly the issue is now on Europe's agenda.
Poland and the Czech Republic, widely tipped as in the first wave of new members, said the move was exactly what they expected. Hungary is also forecast as an early entrant.
Others less sure of immediate membership began a long lobbying campaign to be considered.
Russia, opposed to seeing its old Warsaw Pact allies swallowed up in a Western security fold, was cool to the announcement, saying it wanted more details.
Clinton on the campaign hustings in Detroit on Tuesday set 1999 as a target date for admitting new members to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

Saying the Iron Curtain must not be replaced "by a veil of indifference", Clinton noted that the date was 50 years after NATO was founded to combat a Soviet threat and 10 years after the Berlin Wall fell, heralding the post-communist era.
Reacting to Russia's objections to NATO enlargement, Clinton repeated the Western view that no country had a veto on the alliance's plans.
Moscow declined to jump on Clinton's remarks.

"I do not want to make a specific comment. All I can do is to repeat our general position that we have a negative attitude to the plans for expanding NATO," Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told reporters.
Eastern Europeans were happier, although many saw the news as just a confirmation of what they have long believed.
"This conforms with Polish expectations, which I have repeatedly expressed to our Western partners," Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on a visit to London.
The first new members in from the former communist bloc creates a potential division that worries some of the other applicants.
Slovenia, which may be in the first group but is by no means certain to be, immediately began arguing its case.
Defence Minister Jelko Kacin noted that Clinton had promised financial help to his country to become compatible with NATO, "thus placing it among the strongest candidates."
Albania, which is far from being accepted, welcomed the Clinton announcement as a boost to membership efforts by former communist countries.
"The enlargement of the alliance is an extension of security and stability in Europe and the world," a statement from President Sali Berisha's office said.
